subject: Reproductive
subtopic: Umbilical cord, urachus, vitelline duct and Meckel diverticulum
vignette: A 22-week fetal ultrasound demonstrates a three-vessel umbilical cord. Doppler analysis shows that one vessel carries oxygenated blood from the placenta toward the fetus, while two vessels carry deoxygenated blood back to the placenta. The oxygenated vessel is traced into the fetal abdomen, where it drains into the inferior vena cava partly through the ductus venosus.
question: Which of the following best describes the fetal umbilical circulation?

options.text: Two umbilical veins carry oxygenated blood to the fetus; one artery returns deoxygenated blood
Two umbilical arteries carry oxygenated blood from the internal iliac arteries to the placenta
Two umbilical arteries carry deoxygenated blood from the fetal internal iliac arteries to the placenta, and one vein returns oxygenated blood to the fetus
One umbilical artery and one vein return deoxygenated blood to the placenta
The umbilical vein drains directly into the fetal right atrium

explanation_correct: The normal umbilical cord contains two umbilical arteries and one umbilical vein. The two arteries carry deoxygenated blood from the fetal internal iliac arteries to the placenta, and the single umbilical vein carries oxygenated blood from the placenta back to the fetus. The umbilical vein drains into the inferior vena cava either through the liver or via the ductus venosus. These vessels are derived from the allantois and are embedded in Wharton jelly.

explanation_incorrect.A: The cord has one umbilical vein and two arteries, not two veins; the single vein carries oxygenated blood to the fetus.
explanation_incorrect.B: The umbilical arteries carry deoxygenated blood away from the fetus toward the placenta; although they arise from the internal iliac arteries, their blood is not oxygenated.
explanation_incorrect.D: There are three vessels in a normal cord, two arteries and one vein, and the vein carries oxygenated blood to the fetus, not deoxygenated blood back to the placenta.
explanation_incorrect.E: The umbilical vein drains into the inferior vena cava via the liver or ductus venosus, not directly into the right atrium.

educationalObjective: The cord has two deoxygenated umbilical arteries to the placenta and one oxygenated umbilical vein to the fetus draining into the IVC.

subject: Reproductive
subtopic: Umbilical cord, urachus, vitelline duct and Meckel diverticulum
vignette: A newborn is noted to have a two-vessel umbilical cord at delivery. The infant also has a congenital heart defect and an abnormal renal ultrasound. The obstetrician documents that the cord contains only a single umbilical artery.
question: Which of the following is clinically associated with a single umbilical artery (two-vessel cord)?

options.text: A completely benign finding with no increased risk of anomalies
Increased risk of congenital and chromosomal anomalies
Guaranteed normal renal development
Increased risk of twin-twin transfusion syndrome
Increased risk of polyhydramnios from impaired fetal swallowing

explanation_correct: A single umbilical artery (two-vessel cord) results from agenesis or atrophy of one umbilical artery and is associated with an increased risk of congenital and chromosomal anomalies. It serves as a marker for underlying fetal malformations, particularly renal, cardiac, and gastrointestinal defects. Its presence warrants a careful fetal anatomic survey. This is distinct from the normal three-vessel cord with two arteries and one vein.

explanation_incorrect.A: A two-vessel cord is not a completely benign normal variant; it is associated with an increased risk of congenital and chromosomal anomalies.
explanation_incorrect.C: Rather than guaranteeing normal renal development, a single umbilical artery should raise suspicion for renal anomalies among other congenital defects.
explanation_incorrect.D: Twin-twin transfusion syndrome is related to vascular anastomoses in monochorionic placentas, not to a single umbilical artery in an individual fetus.
explanation_incorrect.E: Polyhydramnios from impaired swallowing is associated with esophageal or duodenal atresia or anencephaly, not with the number of umbilical cord vessels.

educationalObjective: A single umbilical artery (two-vessel cord) is associated with congenital and chromosomal anomalies.

subject: Reproductive
subtopic: Umbilical cord, urachus, vitelline duct and Meckel diverticulum
vignette: A developmental biology student is studying the origin of the umbilical cord vessels and the surrounding gelatinous matrix. The vessels derive from an extraembryonic structure that extends from the yolk sac into the cloaca, and the cord is cushioned by a specialized connective tissue.
question: Which of the following statements about the umbilical cord is correct?

options.text: The umbilical vessels are derived from the amnion and are suspended in Wharton jelly
Wharton jelly is the embryonic precursor of the urachus
The umbilical arteries are derived from yolk sac endoderm without an allantoic intermediate
The umbilical cord normally contains a single artery and two veins
The umbilical vessels are derived from the allantois and are embedded in Wharton jelly

explanation_correct: The umbilical arteries and vein are derived from the allantois, an outpouching of the yolk sac that extends into the cloaca. The umbilical cord contains these vessels embedded in Wharton jelly, a gelatinous connective tissue that cushions and protects them. The allantois's intra-abdominal remnant is the urachus, linking the fetal bladder to the umbilicus. Together these relationships explain the spectrum of urachal remnants.

explanation_incorrect.A: The umbilical vessels are not derived from the amnion; they arise from the allantois, although Wharton jelly does surround them.
explanation_incorrect.B: Wharton jelly is the gelatinous matrix of the cord, not the precursor of the urachus; the urachus is derived from the allantois.
explanation_incorrect.C: The umbilical vessels are associated specifically with the allantois, an endodermal outpouching of the yolk sac; describing them as arising directly from yolk sac endoderm without the allantoic intermediate misses the key embryologic association.
explanation_incorrect.D: The normal cord contains two arteries and one vein, not one artery and two veins.

educationalObjective: Umbilical cord vessels derive from the allantois and are cushioned by Wharton jelly.

subject: Reproductive
subtopic: Umbilical cord, urachus, vitelline duct and Meckel diverticulum
vignette: An adult patient undergoes abdominal surgery. The surgeon identifies a fibrous cord extending from the dome of the urinary bladder to the umbilicus, covered by a peritoneal fold. It is explained that this is the obliterated remnant of a fetal structure that connected the bladder to the umbilicus.
question: What is the adult remnant of the obliterated urachus?

options.text: Median umbilical ligament
Medial umbilical ligament
Round ligament of the liver
Ligamentum teres
Umbilical artery

explanation_correct: The urachus is the intra-abdominal remnant of the allantois, forming a duct between the fetal bladder and the umbilicus. When it obliterates after birth, it becomes the median umbilical ligament, which is covered by the median umbilical fold of peritoneum. This is distinct from the medial umbilical ligaments, which are the obliterated umbilical arteries. Failure of the urachus to involute completely can lead to patent urachus, urachal cyst, or vesicourachal diverticulum.

explanation_incorrect.B: The medial umbilical ligaments are the obliterated umbilical arteries, not the urachus; they lie more laterally in the anterior abdominal wall.
explanation_incorrect.C: The round ligament of the liver is the obliterated umbilical vein, located in the falciform ligament, not the remnant of the urachus.
explanation_incorrect.D: Ligamentum teres is another name for the round ligament of the liver, the obliterated umbilical vein, not the urachus.
explanation_incorrect.E: The umbilical artery is a paired vessel that becomes the medial umbilical ligament when obliterated; it is not the urachus.

educationalObjective: The obliterated urachus becomes the median umbilical ligament; umbilical arteries become the medial umbilical ligaments.

subject: Reproductive
subtopic: Umbilical cord, urachus, vitelline duct and Meckel diverticulum
vignette: A 3-day-old newborn has clear fluid leaking continuously from the umbilicus. The fluid resembles urine, and analysis shows a high urea and creatinine content. Ultrasound shows normal bladder and kidneys, and the tract is traced from the bladder dome to the umbilical opening.
question: Which of the following developmental anomalies best explains this presentation?

options.text: Patent vitelline duct
Urachal cyst
Vesicourachal diverticulum
Patent urachus
Meckel diverticulum

explanation_correct: A patent urachus results from total failure of the urachus to obliterate, leaving an open duct between the fetal bladder and the umbilicus. This allows urine to drain from the bladder and exit at the umbilicus, producing the described urinary discharge. The urachus is the intra-abdominal remnant of the allantois. Untreated urachal remnants can increase the risk of infection and, rarely, malignancy such as adenocarcinoma.

explanation_incorrect.A: A patent vitelline duct would produce meconium discharge from the umbilicus, not urine, because it connects the yolk sac to the midgut lumen.
explanation_incorrect.B: A urachal cyst is a fluid-filled cavity lined by uroepithelium between the umbilicus and bladder; it does not drain continuously to the outside.
explanation_incorrect.C: A vesicourachal diverticulum is a slight failure of obliteration producing an outpouching of the bladder, not an open communication to the umbilicus with continuous urinary drainage.
explanation_incorrect.E: Meckel diverticulum is a true diverticulum of the ileum from incomplete vitelline duct obliteration and causes melena or hematochezia, not urinary discharge from the umbilicus.

educationalObjective: Patent urachus is total failure of urachal obliteration, causing urine discharge from the umbilicus.

subject: Reproductive
subtopic: Umbilical cord, urachus, vitelline duct and Meckel diverticulum
vignette: A 6-year-old child presents with a painful, reddish mass in the lower midline just below the umbilicus that is warm and tender. Ultrasound shows a fluid-filled cavity in the midline between the umbilicus and the bladder, with no open connection to either structure. Histology after drainage reveals a lining of uroepithelium.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Patent urachus
Vesicourachal diverticulum
Omphalocele
Vitelline duct cyst
Infected urachal cyst

explanation_correct: A urachal cyst results from partial failure of the urachus to obliterate, leaving a fluid-filled cavity lined with uroepithelium located between the umbilicus and the bladder. When infected, it presents as a painful, tender mass below the umbilicus, sometimes with erythema. Unlike a patent urachus, it has no open communication to the bladder or umbilicus, so there is no urinary drainage. Urachal remnants may increase infection and malignancy risk if left untreated.

explanation_incorrect.A: A patent urachus is a total failure of obliteration with an open bladder-to-umbilicus channel and urinary discharge, not a closed, infected fluid collection.
explanation_incorrect.B: A vesicourachal diverticulum is a slight failure producing an outpouching continuous with the bladder lumen, not a separate closed cyst between bladder and umbilicus.
explanation_incorrect.C: Omphalocele is a congenital abdominal wall defect with herniation of abdominal contents covered by a membrane, centered at the umbilicus, not a midline uroepithelial-lined cyst.
explanation_incorrect.D: A vitelline duct cyst arises from the omphalomesenteric duct, is associated with volvulus risk, and relates to the gut rather than the bladder-to-umbilicus urachal remnant.

educationalObjective: An infected urachal cyst is a partial urachal obliteration failure presenting as a painful infraumbilical midline mass.

subject: Reproductive
subtopic: Umbilical cord, urachus, vitelline duct and Meckel diverticulum
vignette: A newborn has fecal-appearing material draining from the umbilicus within the first days of life. The discharge contains meconium, and imaging shows a communication between the umbilicus and the midgut. The clinician notes that the structure involved normally closes during the seventh week of development.
question: Which of the following developmental failures is responsible for this presentation?

options.text: Total failure of the vitelline duct to obliterate
Slight failure of the vitelline duct to obliterate
Total failure of the urachus to obliterate
Partial failure of the urachus to obliterate
Failure of the allantois to form the umbilical vessels

explanation_correct: The vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct connects the yolk sac to the midgut lumen and normally obliterates during the seventh week of development. Total failure of the vitelline duct to obliterate produces a patent vitelline duct, creating an open communication between the midgut and the umbilicus through which meconium can discharge. This is distinct from Meckel diverticulum, which is only a slight failure leaving an ileal outpouching. A vitelline duct cyst represents partial failure and carries a volvulus risk.

explanation_incorrect.B: Slight failure of the vitelline duct to obliterate produces Meckel diverticulum, an outpouching of the ileum, not an open umbilical-midgut communication with meconium drainage.
explanation_incorrect.C: Total failure of the urachus to obliterate produces a patent urachus with urinary, not meconium, discharge from the umbilicus.
explanation_incorrect.D: Partial failure of the urachus produces a urachal cyst, a uroepithelial-lined midline fluid collection, not a gut communication with meconium discharge.
explanation_incorrect.E: The allantois forms the umbilical vessels and urachus; failure of the allantois is not the basis of a patent vitelline duct, which derives from the yolk sac-midgut connection.

educationalObjective: Patent vitelline duct is total failure of omphalomesenteric duct obliteration, causing meconium discharge from the umbilicus.

subject: Reproductive
subtopic: Umbilical cord, urachus, vitelline duct and Meckel diverticulum
vignette: A 9-year-old child presents with painless rectal bleeding and melena-like stools. A technetium-99m pertechnetate scan shows focal uptake in the right lower abdomen. Surgical resection reveals a true diverticulum of the ileum containing heterotopic gastric mucosa.
question: Which of the following best explains the origin and consequences of this lesion?

options.text: Total failure of the urachus to obliterate, leading to urinary leakage into the gut
Partial failure of the vitelline duct to obliterate with increased volvulus risk but no bleeding
Slight failure of the vitelline duct to obliterate with heterotopic gastric or pancreatic tissue causing melena and abdominal pain
Failure of the midgut to return from the physiologic omphalocele, producing a patent omphalomesenteric duct
Patency of the ductus arteriosus allowing oxygenated blood to shunt into the gastrointestinal tract

explanation_correct: Meckel diverticulum results from slight (incomplete) failure of the vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct to obliterate, leaving a true diverticulum of the ileum that contains all layers of the bowel wall. It often contains heterotopic gastric and/or pancreatic tissue, whose acid and enzymatic secretion can cause painless hematochezia, melena, or abdominal pain. The rule of 2s (about 2% of the population, 2 feet from the ileocecal valve, 2 inches long, 2 types of heterotopic tissue, symptomatic before age 2, twice as common in males) is a classic association. Technetium pertechnetate scan detects the gastric mucosa.

explanation_incorrect.A: The urachus is the allantoic remnant between bladder and umbilicus; its failure produces urinary discharge or urachal cysts, not an ileal diverticulum causing gastrointestinal bleeding.
explanation_incorrect.B: Partial failure of the vitelline duct produces a vitelline duct cyst with increased volvulus risk, but it is not a true ileal diverticulum with heterotopic gastric mucosa causing melena.
explanation_incorrect.D: Failure of the midgut to return from the physiologic omphalocele produces omphalocele, not Meckel diverticulum, which is a residual of the vitelline duct itself.
explanation_incorrect.E: The ductus arteriosus is a cardiovascular fetal shunt between the aorta and pulmonary artery; it has no relationship to a vitelline duct remnant or lower gastrointestinal bleeding.

educationalObjective: Meckel diverticulum is a slight vitelline duct obliteration failure with heterotopic gastric or pancreatic tissue causing painless GI bleeding.
